c.tagline: Pink-stone Baroque cathedrals and silver-mine history stacked up a high-desert ravine.

taxi.fareNote: Zacatecas taxis are generally not metered - agree the fare before setting off. Uber and DiDi both operate and give an up-front price, though the compact center is easiest on foot.

emergency.note: 911 is Mexico's unified emergency number for police, fire and ambulance; 078 is the national tourist assistance line.

avoid.reason: Stay within the compact historic centre and avoid peripheral colonias and, above all, intercity highways after dark, as Zacatecas state sees serious cartel-related violence.
Petty theft can occur in markets and bus stations, so keep valuables discreet and use registered taxis at night.

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed colonial heart, a warren of pink-cantera-stone streets and callejones around the Baroque cathedral, Plaza de Armas and Hidalgo Avenue; where most museums, restaurants and the nightly callejoneada street parties are, and the best base for first-timers.

An upscale, quieter district along the old El Cubo aqueduct and the Sierra de Alica gardens, home to the landmark Quinta Real hotel built inside a 19th-century bullring; good for a refined, restful stay near the center.

The neighboring colonial town 7 km east, known for the magnificent Convento de Guadalupe and its museum of viceregal art, plus modern shopping malls and business hotels; a calmer, more spread-out place to sleep.

water.note: Drink bottled or purified water only.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 06:00-22:00; the Teleferico operates about 10:00-18:00 daily, weather permitting (it stops in high winds).
transit.note: Zacatecas has no metro or light rail; the compact UNESCO center is best explored on foot, with city buses and taxis or ride apps for longer trips and the Teleferico linking the two hilltops for the views.
transit.pay: City bus fares (~MXN 9-10) are paid in cash to the driver; there is no rechargeable transit card. The Teleferico aerial tram is a tourist attraction with its own ticket, bought at the Cerro del Grillo or Cerro de la Bufa stations.

food.name: Asado de boda zacatecano
food.desc: The wedding roast: pork simmered in a dark chile ancho sauce with a whisper of chocolate and orange, sweet, smoky and unique to Zacatecas.

places.name: El Recoveco
places.note: Long-running buffet of Zacatecan home cooking; the asado de boda is the dish people come for.

places.name: Los Dorados de Villa
places.note: Revolution-themed dining room serving the classic regional menu to locals and visitors alike.

places.name: Asadero El Moral
places.note: Neighbourhood specialist whose whole reputation rests on asado de boda by the kilo.

food.name: Gorditas zacatecanas
food.desc: Thick corn pockets cooked on a comal and split open for stews: chicharron in salsa verde, deshebrada, rajas con queso, nopales or beans.

places.name: Gorditas Dona Julia
places.note: Zacatecas institution with a wall of clay pots of guisados; go early for the widest choice.

places.name: Gorditas El Guero
places.note: Locals rate the thick masa base and generous stews; also does bocoles.

places.name: Mercado Arroyo de la Plata
places.note: Cluster of comal stands where the gorditas are pressed in front of you.

food.name: Birria de chivo
food.desc: Goat marinated in dried chiles and slow-steamed until falling apart, served as a soupy bowl with lime and onion or drained into tacos.

places.name: Birrieria Don Polo
places.note: Tucked at the back of the market; a favourite for goat birria in caldo or in tacos.

places.name: El Recoveco
places.note: Reliable sit-down version of birria alongside the rest of the regional spread.

places.name: Mercado Arroyo de la Plata
places.note: Several rival birria counters under one roof; weekend mornings are the moment.

food.name: Enchiladas zacatecanas
food.desc: Tortillas dipped in a guajillo chile sauce, filled with fresh cheese and onion, fried and crowned with potato and carrot cooked in the same chile.

places.name: Los Dorados de Villa
places.note: Does the full plate with the chile-stained potatoes and carrots on the side.

places.name: El Recoveco
places.note: Part of the rotating buffet of Zacatecan classics; easy way to try several at once.

places.name: Mercado Arroyo de la Plata
places.note: Market fondas turn these out cheaply all morning.

food.name: Queso asadero y quesadillas de queso ranchero
food.desc: Zacatecas is ranching country; its stretchy asadero and crumbly queso ranchero go into griddled quesadillas, chiles rellenos and molten queso fundido.

places.name: Mercado Arroyo de la Plata
places.note: Cheese vendors sell asadero by the wheel and griddle quesadillas to order.

places.name: Gorditas Dona Julia
places.note: Rajas con queso gordita is the easiest way to taste the local cheese.

places.name: Los Dorados de Villa
places.note: Queso fundido and chiles rellenos made with regional cheese.

food.name: Dulces zacatecanos
food.desc: Sweets from the mining era: milky jamoncillo, cajeta de membrillo, candied biznaga and pistachio-studded blocks sold by the slab.

places.name: Mercado Arroyo de la Plata
places.note: Sweet stalls with jamoncillo, ate de membrillo and crystallised fruit.

places.name: Portales de Plaza de Armas
places.note: Arcade shops beside the cathedral selling boxed regional sweets to take home.

food.name: Mezcal zacatecano
food.desc: Zacatecas is a denomination-of-origin mezcal state; its agaves give a mineral, earthy spirit sipped neat with orange and sal de gusano.

places.name: Las Quince Letras
places.note: Cantina-mezcaleria off the pedestrian centre with a deep list of state mezcals.

places.name: El Malacate
places.note: Bar built inside the old silver mine; a memorable place for a mezcal after the tour.

places.name: Mercado Arroyo de la Plata
places.note: Licoreria stalls sell small-batch state mezcal and let you taste first.

food.name: Ponche de granada
food.desc: Sweet pomegranate liqueur from nearby Jerez, poured as a small warming glass; quince, walnut and prickly pear versions sit beside it.

places.name: Mercado Arroyo de la Plata
places.note: Bottled ponche from Jerez producers, usually with a taster poured for you.

places.name: Portales de Plaza de Armas
places.note: Souvenir and liquor shops under the arcades stock the classic red bottles.

landmarks: Zacatecas Cathedral
A pink-stone cathedral whose Churrigueresque facade is carved so exuberantly it ranks among the supreme masterpieces of Mexican Baroque.
Cerro de la Bufa
The craggy hill dominating the city, topped by a Pancho Villa equestrian monument, a chapel, a revolution museum and dizzying miradors.
Mina El Edén
Descend into a legendary silver mine by mine train, exploring tunnels that bankrolled the Spanish Empire—and now conceal an underground nightclub.
Teleférico de Zacatecas
A Swiss-built cable car gliding 650 meters over pink-domed rooftops between Cerro del Grillo and Cerro de la Bufa.
Museo Rafael Coronel
Thousands of Mexican ceremonial masks fill the romantic ruins of the former Convent of San Francisco—an unforgettable, dreamlike collection.
Museo Pedro Coronel
A colonial seminary holding a world-class trove of Picasso, Miró, Dalí and Goya assembled by the Zacatecan painter Pedro Coronel.
Templo de Santo Domingo
A Jesuit-built Baroque church of 1749 with sumptuous gilded retablos, standing on one of the old city's loveliest small plazas.
Ex-Templo de San Agustín
A deconsecrated Augustinian church in the historic center, its spectacular carved plateresque portal now framing an atmospheric exhibition space.
Acueducto El Cubo
A graceful 18th-century pink-stone aqueduct marching beside Enrique Estrada park, one of the silver city's most photographed signature silhouettes.
Plaza de Armas & Palacio de Gobierno
The colonial heart of the city, where murals inside the governor's palace recount four centuries of Zacatecas history beside the cathedral.

train.note: No passenger trains serve Zacatecas; the historic silver-route railway now carries freight only. Travel is by coach or by air into the small airport north of the city.

bus.note: No international coaches. The Central Camionera south of the centre has Ómnibus de México, ETN (https://www.etn.com.mx/) and Futura services to Mexico City in about 8 hours, Guadalajara (5), Aguascalientes (2) and Durango (4-5). Local buses and the Teleférico cable car handle travel within the steep old town.

ferry.note: Zacatecas sits at 2,400 m in the arid northern highlands with no navigable water, so there are no ferries.

half.name: La Quemada (Chicomostoc)
half.blurb: Pre-Hispanic hilltop ruins of stone platforms and a colonnaded hall built by an unidentified ancient culture.

half.name: Jerez de García Salinas
half.blurb: Colonial town with a 19th-century theater and a well-preserved historic center of stone arcades.

full.name: Sombrerete
full.blurb: Former silver-mining town with baroque churches and colonial mansions built on mining wealth.
